title: mpy_ld.py: Unsupported relocation when using cos/sin functions
body:
### Checks

- [X] I agree to follow the MicroPython [Code of Conduct](https://github.com/micropython/micropython/blob/master/CODEOFCONDUCT.md) to ensure a safe and respectful space for everyone.

- [X] I've searched for [existing issues](https://github.com/micropython/micropython/issues) matching this bug, and didn't find any.


### Port, board and/or hardware

esp32/xtensawin and armv7emsp

### MicroPython version

MicroPython 1.22.2 from git

### Reproduction

1. Have a dynamic native module using sinf/cosf functions

Note, you have to include the object files from libm and libgcc manually in the Makefile. This means extracting the .o files from the archives, and then adding them to SRC_O make variable. See this for an example:
https://github.com/emlearn/emlearn-micropython/blob/bd85ae1fade99b34a626c9fcaae0aa4f2ec87803/src/emlfft/Makefile

```
ifeq ($(ARCH), xtensawin)
    LIBM_O := lib_a-sf_cos.o lib_a-sf_sin.o lib_a-ef_rem_pio2.o lib_a-kf_cos.o lib_a-kf_sin.o lib_a-sf_fabs.o lib_a-kf_rem_pio2.o lib_a-sf_scalbn.o lib_a-sf_floor.o
endif
ifeq ($(ARCH), armv7emsp)
    LIBM_O := libm_a-sf_cos.o libm_a-sf_sin.o libm_a-ef_rem_pio2.o libm_a-kf_cos.o libm_a-kf_sin.o libm_a-sf_fabs.o libm_a-kf_rem_pio2.o libm_a-sf_scalbn.o libm_a-sf_floor.o
endif

ifeq ($(ARCH), armv7emsp)
	SOFTFP_O := _arm_addsubdf3.o _arm_muldivdf3.o _arm_muldivdf3.o _arm_truncdfsf2.o
endif
ifeq ($(ARCH), xtensawin)
	SOFTFP_O := _floatsidf.o _muldf3.o _divdf3.o _truncdfsf2.o
endif
```

2. Try to build the module

### Expected behaviour

Linking succeeds without errors, module is functional.

Alternatively: Error and/or documentation provides hints as to the possible reasons why this could happen, and ways of resolving.

### Observed behaviour

Exception when linking. With ARCH=xtensawin

```
  File "/home/<user>/projects/micropython/tools/mpy_ld.py", line 572, in do_relocation_text
    assert 0, r_info_type
AssertionError: 11
```

On ARCH=armv7emsp
```
  File "/home/<user>/projects/micropython/tools/mpy_ld.py", line 572, in do_relocation_text
    assert 0, r_info_type
AssertionError: 2
```

### Additional Information

arm-none-eabi-gcc --version
arm-none-eabi-gcc (Arch Repository) 13.2.0

xtensa-esp32-elf-gcc --version
xtensa-esp32-elf-gcc (crosstool-NG esp-2022r1) 11.2.0

comments.author: reporter
comments.body:
I am aware that I am pushing the mpy_ld.py / dynamic module support quite hard here, compared to usual. But some tips as to what might be the issue here would be very welcomed. So that maybe we can improve the support. 

I am providing here the .o files for the `__ieee754_rem_pio2f` (for xtensawin and armv7emsp). I have poked a bit with readelf/objdump, but don't really know how to interpret the relocations - and why this symbol is different from any others...
[micropython-reloc-rem_pio2.zip](https://github.com/micropython/micropython/files/15212504/micropython-reloc-rem_pio2.zip)

comments.author: reporter
comments.body: Renamed issue to highlight relevance. I am pretty sure this would happen whenever sin/cos or sinf/cosf are used. It would happen also if there just exists some code calling these functions - even these code paths are not actually used. Because there seems to be no dead-code stripping done by mpy_ld.py.

@reporter Does this patch fix the issue for Xtensa/Xtensawin?

```diff
--- mpy_ld.py.orig      2024-08-18 20:44:32.381793792 +0200
+++ mpy_ld.py   2024-08-18 20:52:20.521190910 +0200
@@ -69,6 +69,7 @@
 R_386_GOTOFF = 9
 R_386_GOTPC = 10
 R_ARM_THM_CALL = 10
+R_XTENSA_ASM_EXPAND = 11
 R_XTENSA_DIFF32 = 19
 R_XTENSA_SLOT0_OP = 20
 R_ARM_BASE_PREL = 25  # aka R_ARM_GOTPC
@@ -562,7 +563,7 @@
         reloc = addr - r_offset
         reloc_type = "xtensa_l32r"

-    elif env.arch.name == "EM_XTENSA" and r_info_type in (R_XTENSA_DIFF32, R_XTENSA_PDIFF32):
+    elif env.arch.name == "EM_XTENSA" and r_info_type in (R_XTENSA_DIFF32, R_XTENSA_PDIFF32, R_XTENSA_ASM_EXPAND):
         if s.section.name.startswith(".text"):
             # it looks like R_XTENSA_[P]DIFF32 into .text is already correctly relocated
             return
```

comments.author: participant1
comments.body: Regarding the assertion on the unhandled relocation, it's a R_ARM_ABS32 relocation that is currently supported only on .data segments but not .text/.rodata.  The fix is easy (take the existing word in the file, add the relocation value, find the target it points to and if it's a `STT_FUNC` symbol that's a thumb function turn bit #0 on), but I can continue to look at it tomorrow.

>   File "tools/mpy_ld.py", line 93, in asm_jump_thumb
>     assert b_off >> 11 == 0 or b_off >> 11 == -1, b_off
> ```

Sorry for getting back to you this late, was busy with other stuff...  Anyway, that should be fixed with this (not tested on HW, when disassembling a MPY file with ghidra the offsets look OK):

```diff
 def asm_jump_thumb(entry):
-    # Only signed values that fit in 12 bits are supported
     b_off = entry - 4
-    assert b_off >> 11 == 0 or b_off >> 11 == -1, b_off
-    return struct.pack("<H", 0xE000 | (b_off >> 1 & 0x07FF))
+    if b_off >> 11 != 0 and b_off >> 11 != -1:
+        # sub   sp, #4
+        # push  {r6, r7}
+        # ldr   r7, [pc, #8]
+        # add   r6, pc, #0
+        # add   r7, r6
+        # str   r7, [sp, #8]
+        # pop   {r6, r7}
+        # pop   {pc}
+        # .word entry - 8
+        return struct.pack(
+            "<HHHHHHHHI", 0xB081, 0xB4C0, 0x4F02, 0xA600, 0x4437, 0x9702, 0xBCC0, 0xBD00, b_off - 4
+        )
+    return struct.pack("<H9H", 0xE000 | (b_off >> 1 & 0x07FF), *([0xDE00] * 9))
```

I'm not as familiar with ARM's EABI calling convention as I used to be, so maybe R6 and R7 don't need to be saved and restored in this case but that can't hurt I guess.  The extra R_ARM_ABS32 relocations need to still be sorted out, but that's for tomorrow!

@participant2 for that relocation type, in theory the fix would be:

```diff
diff --git a/tools/mpy_ld.py b/tools/mpy_ld.py
index 56714a3cd..29ec51e0b 100755
--- a/tools/mpy_ld.py
+++ b/tools/mpy_ld.py
@@ -568,6 +580,11 @@ def do_relocation_text(env, text_addr, r):
             return
         assert 0
 
+    elif env.arch.name == "EM_ARM" and r_info_type == R_ARM_ABS32:
+        addr = s.section.addr + s["st_value"]
+        reloc = addr + r_addend
+        reloc_type = "le32"
+
     else:
         # Unknown/unsupported relocation
         assert 0, r_info_type
```

although I'm not sure it's correct in practice - feel free to try it but I doubt it'll work.

(*Take all the following with a grain of salt, if the patch works then great - ignore the rest, if it doesn't work, well, maybe that's why*)

Take for example the first instance of such a relocation in divdf3.o (inside __aeabi_ddiv) once packed into `coremark.mpy`:

```asm

00100d6a 9b 00        lsls  r3,r3,#0x2                     ; Address word-sized values
00100d6c cb 58        ldr   r3,[r1,r3]                     ; Get lookup table entry
                      ; Something else should be added here to add the value of the

001012b4 b0 0d 00 00  ddw   DB0h                           ; are correctly relocated, they do
001012b8 8e 0d 00 00  ddw   D8Eh                           ; have a relocation entry each,
001012bc a2 0e 00 00  ddw   EA2h                           ; though...
001012c0 8e 0d 00 00  ddw   D8Eh
```

So, the linker replaces the opcodes at 0x100D68 and 0x100D6E into something else for that relocation?  No idea, really.

Changing the opcodes in the object file is doable although not easy, you'd have to write a tool to rearrange relocation offsets to reflect the new instruction block lengths.  Not sure if `pyelftools` can also let you *write* object files rather than just reading/parsing them.  If it does then great, just change all R_ARM_ABS32 relocations in .text segments into something else and patch the object files - you're already supplying your own runtime object files :)

comments.body:
The object files I used to build `coremark.mpy` are here: [libgcc-armv6m.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/16880570/libgcc-armv6m.zip) - I've taken them out from `/usr/lib/gcc/arm-none-eabi/14.1.0/thumb/v6-m/nofp/libgcc.a` provided by Arch Linux's `extra/arm-none-eabi-gcc` package.  Still, I'll see if I can get a cheap RPi board here to eventually try that out with a JTAG debugger attached.

For the ESP8266 bit, I admit I don't have much experience with that but I can see two possible solutions.

If you have object files that reference the symbols present in ROM, you can patch `mpy_ld.py` to fill in the new jump address for those symbols (must be PC-relative) when they are encountered in `R_XTENSA_32` relocations.  The ROM addresses are in `$SDKROOT/ld/eagle.rom.addr.v6.ld`.

The other option would be to create simple Xtensa assembler functions that only contain the jump opcode to the target function's address in the ROM, then compile it with `xtensa-lx106-elf-as` and bring it in your build.  So, for example if you only want to provide `memcpy` and `memset` you can compile this into an object file and link it as part of your MPY file (WARNING: UNTESTED - I'll give it a try tomorrow morning):

```asm
	.file   "stdlib.s"
	.text
	
	.align  4

	.global memcpy
	.type   memcpy, @function
memcpy:
	j       0x4000DF48
	.size   memcpy, .-memcpy

	.align  4       // Not sure if this is needed after the first one but it won't hurt.
	
	.global memset
	.type   memset, @function
memset:
	j       0x4000E190
	.size   memset, .-memset
```

`xtensa-lx106-elf-as` will generate `R_XTENSA_SLOT0_OP` relocations for each of the final addresses, which `mpy_ld.py` should already handle.

Again, none of these approaches have been tested, but rather than starting to patch `mpy_ld.py`, I'd do some experiments with the hand-written trampolines file first.  Once you get a working .mpy file you can get the code block offset via `mpy-tool.py -dx $FILE` (the first blue byte in the colourised output), then cut that bit away from the file and use either `xtensa-lx106-elf-objdump` (cannot remember the flags to let it disassemble a raw binary) to see what's going on or, what I use, open the .mpy file with a build of [Ghidra](https://github.com/nationalsecurityagency/ghidra) taken from Git master.  For Ghidra you can just enter the start offset and pick the Xtensa CPU for disassembly when opening the file.  Just don't leave 0 as a starting code address, but pick something like 0x100000 instead (makes it easier to see if offsets have been patched or left alone).

Hope that helps, I'll try this out tomorrow anyway and see how far I get :)

comments.body:
@participant2 I managed to let the debugger work (of course that had to happen *right after* the notification the new SWD/JTAG probe shipped, oh well).

So, what shows up in gdb is the native code runs, then the bytecode vm kicks in, and somehow it ends trashing both the stack and the program counter, with the MCU executing the address of one of the bytecode handlers as if it were Arm opcodes.

```
(gdb) bt

#0  HardFault_Handler () at /micropython/lib/pico-sdk/src/rp2_common/pico_standard_link/crt0.S:98
#1  <signal handler called>
   0xfffffff9:
Cannot access memory at address 0xfffffff8
#2  0x700a3128 in ?? ()
#3  0x100544d0 in __func__.0 ()
Backtrace stopped: previous frame identical to this frame (corrupt stack?)
(gdb) x/8a $sp

0x20041c90:     (R0) 0x0     (R1) 0x700a3128      (R2) 0x0     (R3) 0x0
0x20041ca0:     (R12) 0xfffffc01      (Return address) 0x100544d0 <entry_table.1>      (Program counter) 0x700a3128      (Cpu state) 0x41000000
```

To figure out exactly where this happens, rather than stepping in for 30 minutes each time, if you have a debug probe you can attach to the RP2040 you can insert breakpoint opcodes to act as checkpoints in the debugger to see where you're at.

The `BKPT` Thumb instruction does exactly that, also taking an 8 bit value as a marker (0xBExx with xx being the marker byte).  I don't know if gdb can take over and continue after that, but if it doesn't and enters into `HardFault_Handler`, you can see the offending instruction address with `x/a $sp + 24`.  If it's between 0x20000000 and 0x20042000, or between 0x10000000 and 0x10200000 then it can be disassembled with `x/i <address>`, so you can see if it's one of your BKPTs.  If it's outside that range, well, then the breakpoint should be placed earlier :)

It sucks, I know.  I guess the alternative is to write your own handler for the `DebugMon` exception, but last time I implemented a recoverable `DebugMon` exception handler was 10+ years ago, and I don't remember if just an empty handler will work or not.  https://developer.arm.com/documentation/ddi0419/e/?lang=en has the answer but I can look at that in a couple of days from now :(

TL;DR: The armv6m object files reference those functions in an unsupported manner (see the explicit limitation on `example/natmod/features2` not being part of the CI process for that platform).

With that out of the way, all the other platforms reference soft-float functions as relative offsets to a common base address.  `mpy_ld.py` then just embeds the correct offset in the opcodes in question at symbol resolution time, since it already collected all known external references, put all them up together in a single chunk and recorded the starting offset to each of them.  At runtime the base address is then set by the native code loader, execution goes to the jump trampoline and off you go.

On armv6m those references end up pointing to *absolute* addresses, so `mpy_ld.py` has no idea on how to handle them, as the final symbol address cannot be known at linking time, but only at runtime.  I assume `ld` performs some opcode rewriting (as part of the linking optimisation pass) to work around this, but that's not what `mpy_ld.py` is actually able to do.  A possible solution to this problem is to provide an extra section in MPY files containing the relative offset for each referenced symbol, together with all locations where they are referenced from, and embedding the correctly computed address into the appropriate opcodes (since the offsets were loaded from the MPY file and you know the relocated code segment's start address) as part of the code loading process.

It is something I may put in my TODO list, but that's after the Xtensa LX6/LX7 inline assembler opcodes support and investigating if SIMD opcodes that are present in the ESP32S3 can be put to some use inside MicroPython.

comments.body:
One thing you may want to try is to use `-fPIC` instead of `-fpic`, as it implies some changes in the memory model (and thus might impact how code is accessed).  `-fPIC` is the non-optimised version of `-fpic` so it should be something worth trying first.

Another thing worth mentioning is that a few floating point stdlib functions are now treated as builtins by GCC, so the way they are accessed may have some implications on what is emitted.  

The first thing that came to mind was that an absolute relocation was emitted in order to reserve enough space to fit a FPU opcode in there if needed when performing the final linking pass, but unless I wade into GCC/binutils source code that's just a (wildly) uneducated guess.

Adding an error message is something that can easily be done, but anyone can do that, just check if the arch is `EM_ARM` and the relocation type is `R_ARM_ABS32`, then print an error message if it's the case :)

comments.body: Absolute relocations can actually be supported by `mpy_ld.py`.  I've implemented that in #17377.  With that PR I can use `sin` and `cos` on `ARCH=armv6m` targets, eg RP2040.

comments.author: participant1
comments.body: @participant3 would it work for cases like https://github.com/micropython/micropython/issues/14430#issuecomment-2326857677 ?

comments.author: participant3
comments.body:
> would it work for cases like [#14430 (comment)](https://github.com/micropython/micropython/issues/14430#issuecomment-2326857677)

Yes, that's exactly the case that now works: when there's a `ldr r1, [pc, #off]` and the data it loads at `pc+#off` has an `R_ARM_ABS32` relocation.  `mpy_ld.py` already supported `R_ARM_ABS32` in the ro-data section, just not in the text section.  The logic is the same though, so all that I needed to do in #17377 was use the existing ro-data relocation logic when in the text section.

The particular case I saw with sin/cos functions was using a constant table of floats (in the text section) whose address needed to be taken and passed to another function.
